title: Quadratic-form order and positive operators
subtitle: G2 lecture 033000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: For an ordinary number, positivity is straightforward.
body: Three is positive, negative two is not, and zero sits at the boundary. For a matrix, it cannot mean that all its entries are positive. A matrix can have negative entries and still be positive in the sense used in operator theory. Conversely, a matrix with all positive entries need not satisfy that operator-theoretic condition. What we need is a definition that survives a change of orthonormal coordinates and tells us how the operator acts on every direction.

slides.title: A matrix as a measurement of energy
slides.lead: Take a real symmetric matrix A and a vector x.
body: Form the number obtained by multiplying x by A and taking the inner product of x with the result. This number is called the quadratic form of A at x. You have already met its normalized version: the Rayleigh quotient. Here we keep the length of x in the expression instead of dividing by it. We call A positive semidefinite when its quadratic form is never negative, no matter which vector we choose. In the complex setting, we use self-adjoint operators and their real-valued quadratic forms. Why require self-adjointness? Because we want an order on operators with the same geometric behavior as the order on real numbers.

slides.title: A matrix with negative entries can be positive
slides.lead: Look at the symmetric matrix with two on both diagonal entries and negative one in both off-diagonal positions.
body: Choose a vector with real coordinates x and y. Its quadratic form is two x squared, minus two x times y, plus two y squared. Rewrite that as the square of x minus y, plus x squared, plus y squared. Each term is nonnegative. Therefore the entire expression is nonnegative for every vector. In fact, it is strictly positive for every nonzero vector. So this matrix is positive definite, although two entries are negative. Now take the diagonal matrix with entries negative one and two. Its entries are easy to inspect, but the important test is directional.

slides.title: The spectral criterion
slides.lead: We can test positivity using the finite spectral theorem.
body: Suppose A is self-adjoint, with an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Write a vector as a sum of components along those directions. Its quadratic form is the sum of each eigenvalue multiplied by the squared length of the corresponding component. If every eigenvalue is nonnegative, each term in that sum is nonnegative. Therefore the operator is positive semidefinite. Conversely, if an eigenvalue is negative, choose a unit eigenvector for it. Its quadratic form equals that negative eigenvalue. So the operator cannot be positive semidefinite.

slides.title: Ordering two operators
slides.lead: Now we can compare matrices using an analogue of the usual number-line order.
body: For two self-adjoint operators A and B on the same space, say that A is less than or equal to B when B minus A is positive semidefinite. Equivalently, for every vector x, the quadratic form of A at x is at most the quadratic form of B at x. This is sometimes called the Loewner order, or quadratic-form order. Notice that it is a partial order. Some pairs of operators cannot be compared in either direction. For example, consider A with diagonal entries one and zero, and B with diagonal entries zero and one. On the first coordinate vector, A gives the larger quadratic form. On the second, B gives the larger one.

slides.title: Order survives changes of coordinates and compression
slides.lead: There is a particularly useful rule.
body: If A is less than or equal to B, and C is any linear map into their space, then C adjoint times A times C is less than or equal to C adjoint times B times C. Let's prove it with one vector. Choose any input vector y for C. The quadratic form of C adjoint A C at y is exactly the quadratic form of A at the vector C y. By our assumption, that is no greater than the quadratic form of B at C y. Rewrite this as the quadratic form of C adjoint B C at y. Since the inequality holds for every y, the operator inequality follows. If C is unitary, this is simply a change of orthonormal coordinates. Positivity must survive because the geometry has not changed.

slides.title: Gram operators are automatically positive
slides.lead: We already constructed Gram operators from linear maps.
body: For any linear map S between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, its source Gram operator is S adjoint times S. Evaluate its quadratic form at x. The result is the inner product of S x with itself: the squared norm of S x. Squared lengths are nonnegative. Therefore S adjoint S is positive semidefinite. The Gram construction encodes lengths and inner products in a positive self-adjoint operator, whose spectrum determines the singular values. The kernel also has a simple interpretation. The quadratic form of S adjoint S vanishes at x exactly when S x is zero. So its zero directions are precisely the kernel of S.

slides.title: Why products require care
slides.lead: It is tempting to say that the product of two positive operators is always positive, just as the product of two nonnegative numbers is nonnegative.
body: That is false unless we impose additional structure. Take the projection A onto the first coordinate axis. Take B to be the matrix with every entry equal to one. Both are positive semidefinite. But the product A B has first row one, one and second row zero, zero. It is not symmetric, so it is not a positive operator in our sense. When positive operators commute, they can be diagonalized together in finite dimensions, and their product is again positive. Without commutation, even self-adjointness of the product can fail.

slides.title: Toward positive square roots
slides.lead: We have learned to detect positivity through quadratic forms and through eigenvalues.
body: We have also learned how to apply functions to self-adjoint operators. Combine those ideas. If A is positive, all its eigenvalues are nonnegative. We can take the ordinary nonnegative square root of each eigenvalue, then reassemble an operator using the same spectral projections. The result will be positive, and squaring it will recover A. But is it the only positive operator whose square is A? And can we characterize it without choosing coordinates? Those are the questions.

slides.title: The mathematical relationship
slides.lead: We have learned to detect positivity through quadratic forms and through eigenvalues.
body: We have also learned how to apply functions to self-adjoint operators. Combine those ideas. If A is positive, all its eigenvalues are nonnegative.

slides.title: What to retain
slides.lead: That reconstruction gives us the tools we will need for positive square roots, the operator modulus, and eventually polar decomposition.
